title: How credentials actually leak
body_md:
## Follow the credential, then interrupt the chain

A leaked address is not the same as a leaked password, and a leaked password is not the same as a successful login. The practical task is to find which secret was exposed, where it was reused, and whether an account still has an active session or recovery route an intruder could use. Do not assume every breach contains readable passwords or that every password hash can be cracked quickly.

### Four routes into an account

A service breach may expose email addresses, password hashes, or other data. A hash is a one-way representation used for verification; its resistance to offline guessing depends on the password and the service's hashing design. Some incidents expose plaintext, and some expose no passwords. Malware on a device can capture credentials or session data as they are used. A fake sign-in page can collect what a person types, sometimes including a one-time code. Finally, attackers can try a known email–password pair on another service: **credential stuffing** works when the password was reused.

A unique generated password confines the damage of one site's leaked password to that site. It does not undo a compromised session or protect a device infected with malware. MFA adds a separate obstacle, but a manually entered code can be relayed through a live phishing page. Passkeys and appropriately configured FIDO security keys resist that particular relay by binding authentication to the service's domain.

### Turn a breach notice into an action list

Open the affected service through a saved bookmark or a new typed address, not the notification's sign-in button. Read its own incident notice: what data was involved, when, and what action it asks for. Change the affected account's password if the provider says it was exposed or if you suspect compromise; if that password was reused, change every reused copy, starting with primary email and financial accounts. Review sessions, recovery methods and MFA on accounts that may have been accessed. If device malware is plausible, clean the device before entering fresh secrets.

Have I Been Pwned (HIBP) can show whether an address appears in its indexed incidents. Its address search does **not** tell you which password belonged to that address, and a missing result is not proof of safety. Never paste a real password into this lesson or a random breach-checking page. Use your manager's trusted health function or the official HIBP documentation if you want to understand password checks.

widget_config.goal: Trace a reported exposure to the accounts that need action without assuming a listed email means a password was stolen.
widget_config.today_action: Review one old breach notice from the provider’s own site; list any reused password locations and replace those passwords from clean, directly opened account pages.
widget_config.scope: General education across jurisdictions; breach details and account controls depend on the provider. Sources checked 2026-10-20.

sources.title: Have I Been Pwned: Frequently Asked Questions
sources.scope: Service documentation; a listed address is not proof that its password leaked; coverage is incomplete.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-63B-4: Authenticators
sources.scope: US federal digital identity technical standard; phishing resistance and authenticator types.

sources.title: FTC: How To Recover Your Hacked Email or Social Media Account
sources.scope: US consumer guidance; provider-specific controls vary.

blocks.title: Forum password reused at a payment service
blocks.situation: A synthetic hobby forum announces that password hashes were taken. Its member used the same password at a payment account, but the payment account has not reported a breach.
blocks.analysis: The forum hash may or may not be cracked; reuse creates the cross-service route. Replace the payment password first, then the forum password, review payment sessions and enable its strongest available MFA. Do not wait for proof of misuse.

blocks.title: A legitimate notice involving only email addresses
blocks.situation: A synthetic library sends a valid incident notice stating that email addresses and reading preferences were exposed, while passwords were not in the affected system.
blocks.analysis: This is still a privacy and targeted-phishing concern, but it does not itself prove a password leak. Verify the notice through the library’s own site, watch for follow-up impersonation, and avoid an unnecessary blanket reset unless other evidence appears.

blocks.title: Triage a small-service exposure
blocks.setup: Synthetic account: a craft forum reports stolen hashes. You once reused its password at an email service and a shop; you are on a trusted device.

steps.prompt: A message offers a “check your password” link. Where do you start?

choices.text: Enter the password on the message’s checker.
choices.consequence: The page now has a reusable secret.
choices.explanation: A breach warning can be copied or forged. Do not give a real password to an unverified page.

choices.text: Open the forum from a saved route and read its incident statement.
choices.consequence: You see the affected data categories without giving the message a login.
choices.explanation: A directly opened provider page can establish what was reported; the message link is not required.

steps.prompt: The forum says hashes may be exposed; the old password was reused for email. Which change comes first?

choices.text: Replace the email password with a unique one and check email MFA.
choices.consequence: The most consequential reuse route is closed.
choices.explanation: Email often receives other accounts’ reset links; priority follows possible impact.

choices.text: Change only the forum password and wait for email alerts.
choices.consequence: The reused email credential remains usable if cracked.
choices.explanation: A forum reset does not change the same password at another service.

steps.prompt: You find an unfamiliar email session. What now?

choices.text: Ignore it because the new password blocks old sessions automatically.
choices.explanation: Session invalidation varies by service; inspect the actual controls.

choices.text: Sign it out through email security settings, inspect recovery and forwarding, then rotate relevant secrets.
choices.consequence: The active route and hidden persistence points are addressed.
choices.explanation: A password change alone may not remove every live session or malicious forwarding rule.

steps.prompt: HIBP has no result for a second address. What can you conclude?

choices.text: Nothing definitive; keep unique passwords and MFA for that address.
choices.consequence: You avoid treating incomplete indexing as a safety certificate.
choices.explanation: HIBP covers indexed incidents, not every exposure or malware event.

choices.text: That address has never been exposed.
choices.consequence: A false assurance stops the audit.
choices.explanation: Absence from one database is not proof of no incident.

blocks.debrief: The chain is exposure → possible password recovery or capture → reuse → account access. Interrupt it at reuse, MFA and session control. Retry any decision before applying the pattern to your own accounts.

questions.prompt: A provider says only email addresses were exposed. What follows?

choices.text: Every password using that address must have leaked.
choices.explanation: An address alone does not prove password exposure.

choices.text: Targeted phishing may increase, but a password leak is not established.
choices.explanation: The disclosed data category matters; verify the provider notice.

questions.prompt: A stolen password hash is useful to an attacker when?

choices.text: It can sometimes be guessed offline, depending on the password and hashing design.
choices.explanation: Hash exposure creates possible offline guessing, not automatic plaintext recovery.

choices.text: It always reveals the original password immediately.
choices.explanation: Hashing does not work as simple reversible encryption.

questions.prompt: Why change a reused password at a second service?

choices.text: A second service automatically shares its database with the first.
choices.explanation: The threat is attempted login with the same credential, not automatic database sharing.

choices.text: The same secret may be tried there even if that service was not breached.
choices.explanation: Credential stuffing crosses service boundaries through reuse.
